common_name: Infinitini Brite Pink Crape Myrtle (Dwarf Patio Bright Pink Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Ideal for small borders, mass plantings, and large patio containers; part of the ultra-dwarf Infinitini series bred for compact, rounded habit.

directions: Infinitini Brite Pink forms a dense, rounded mound smothered in clusters of bright pink, crinkled flowers from early summer into fall. Its compact two-to-four-foot size fits containers and small-space borders where full-size crape myrtles would quickly outgrow the spot. Foliage emerges with a bronzy tint before maturing to glossy green. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and avoid heavy pruning since flowers form on new wood.

common_name: Infinitini Orchid Crape Myrtle (Dwarf Patio Lavender-Purple Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Low, arching habit suits containers and small borders; part of the Infinitini series of ultra-dwarf crape myrtles.

directions: Infinitini Orchid produces a low, gently arching mound covered in showy lavender-purple flower clusters through the heat of summer. Its spread is noticeably wider than it is tall, giving a mounded rather than upright form that works well spilling over container edges or massed as a low hedge. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, and leave pruning minimal since bloom develops on new growth. This selection has become harder to find commercially as the Infinitini lineup has been refreshed with newer colors.

common_name: Center Stage Pink Crape Myrtle (Dark-Leaved Hot Pink Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Center Stage Pink was selected through University of Florida breeding trials for early bloom and intensified near-black foliage color.

directions: Center Stage Pink carries hot pink, crepe-paper flower clusters set against dramatic reddish-black foliage that holds its dark color through the growing season. It blooms earlier in the summer than many standard crape myrtles and keeps flowering heavily into fall. The exfoliating bark adds winter interest once leaves drop. Grow in full sun with good drainage; the series was bred for improved resistance to powdery mildew compared with older crape myrtle cultivars.

common_name: Ebony and Ivory Crape Myrtle (Black-Leaved White-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; bred jointly by USDA-ARS (Cecile Pounders) and Mississippi State University, released 2013, from a cross of 'Whit VII' (Siren Red) and 'Chocolate Mocha' (Delta Jazz).

directions: Ebony and Ivory pairs near-black foliage, emerging coppery-bronze in spring before darkening, with panicles of frilly, yellowish-white flowers held at the branch tips from late spring into early fall. The strong color contrast between dark leaves and pale blooms makes it a standout specimen or accent shrub. It grows as a dense, multi-stemmed, upright-spreading shrub with notably clean foliage, having been bred specifically for disease resistance. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and prune minimally since flowers form on new wood.

common_name: Early Bird White Crape Myrtle (Early-Blooming Reblooming White Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; selected for an unusually early bloom start that continues through the growing season.

directions: Early Bird White begins flowering notably earlier in the season than most crape myrtles, typically opening its first pure white blooms in May and continuing in flushes into fall. Its dense, upright habit reaches five to eight feet tall on a narrower three-to-four-foot base, making it useful where height is wanted without a wide footprint. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and avoid heavy pruning, since the extended bloom period depends on continuous new growth. It was discovered as a seedling selection in Florida by John McNair Davy and is part of a trio of Early Bird introductions prized for jumping the gun on the usual midsummer crape myrtle season.

common_name: Early Bird Lavender Crape Myrtle (Early-Blooming Weeping-Habit Lavender Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; a semi-dwarf Early Bird series selection with an unusually long May-to-September bloom window.

directions: Early Bird Lavender opens soft lavender flower clusters as early as May and keeps blooming for months, far longer than typical midsummer-only crape myrtles. Branches have a distinctive spreading-to-weeping form that arches gracefully as the plant matures, setting it apart from the stiffly upright habit of most cultivars. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; it was discovered as an open-pollinated seedling in a planting of 'Yuma' crape myrtles in Florida and selected for its unusual bloom timing and habit. Prune lightly, since flowers form on new wood throughout the long season.

common_name: Early Bird Purple Crape Myrtle (Early-Blooming Frilly Purple Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; discovered as a seedling selection among openly pollinated 'Zuni' crape myrtles in Florida.

directions: Early Bird Purple carries dense clusters of ruffled, frilly purple flowers from May through frost, giving one of the longest bloom seasons among crape myrtles. Its dense, upright growth reaches five to eight feet tall while staying narrow at three to four feet wide, suiting it to tighter planting spaces than wide-spreading cultivars. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil and prune lightly in late winter to maintain shape, since the extended flowering depends on steady new growth through the season.

common_name: Let's Dance Rhapsody Blue Hydrangea (Reblooming Blue-to-Pink Mophead Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a Let's Dance series selection that reblooms on new wood after old-wood buds are lost to winter.

directions: Let's Dance Rhapsody Blue produces large mophead flower clusters that shift from rich sapphire blue in acidic soil to vivid pink in more alkaline soil, following the usual aluminum-availability pattern of bigleaf hydrangeas. It flowers on both old and new wood, so plants still bloom reliably in June through August even after a winter that damages old stems. Keep the root zone consistently moist and mulched, siting it in full sun to partial shade with afternoon shade in hot climates. Prune only to remove dead wood right after the first flush to preserve old-wood buds for the next round of bloom.

common_name: Tuff Stuff Top Fun Hydrangea (Burgundy-Stemmed Reblooming Mountain Hydrangea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; a Tuff Stuff series mountain hydrangea noted for bright burgundy stems supporting its lacecap blooms.

directions: Tuff Stuff Top Fun bears bold lacecap flower heads in blue, purple, or pink tones depending on soil acidity, carried on bright burgundy stems that add contrast even before bloom. Like other Tuff Stuff mountain hydrangeas, it flowers on both old and new wood, giving it more dependable rebloom in colder zones than bigleaf types that rely mainly on old wood. Its compact two-to-three-foot habit suits small gardens and foundation plantings. Grow in full sun to part sun in moist, well-drained soil, and limit pruning to spent blooms since the plant needs little shaping.
